title: Right in his own eyes (Judges 21:25)
hook: the book ends: "every man did that which was right in his own eyes"

segments.voice: Yesterday, Samson at the pillars, asking for strength only this once. Your line was only this once. Did you ask for help when you were running low? Today, the book of Judges closes. Day seven hundred twenty-six.

Here is the last verse of the book of Judges: "In those days there was no king in Israel; every man did that which was right in his own eyes." That's it. No song, no victory, no wedding. The last chapters before it are hard to read: a private shrine with a hired priest, a tribe that carries off that shrine's idols and its priest, a crime in a city at night, and a war between the tribes that nearly wipes one of them out. And then that sentence, like a door closing.
screen: `NO SONG, NO VICTORY.` → `HARD CHAPTERS.` → `A DOOR CLOSING.`

segments.voice: The line isn't new. It has been coming back in those last chapters like a refrain: in those days there was no king in Israel. The text keeps saying it. And the full sentence, everyone doing what was right in his own eyes, stands at both ends of those chapters: as they open, and as the very last line. The phrase has a history. In Deuteronomy, Moses tells the people that in the land they will not do as they do now, every man whatever is right in his own eyes. Instead, the Torah says, do what is right and good in the eyes of the Lord. Same words, other eyes. And there's an echo inside Judges. When Samson first sees a Philistine woman and wants to marry her, he tells his father, get her for me, and in Hebrew what he says is: she is right in my eyes. The man who went after his eyes, in the book that ends with everyone doing what was right in their own. What does the closing line want? Readers differ. Some hear a call for a king, and the next book brings one. Others remember that Gideon refused a crown, saying the Lord shall rule over you, and they hear the problem as people with no one to answer to but themselves. Either way, the book ends on a warning about people who answer to no one but themselves. In its telling, a person's own eyes are real, and they matter, but they are not enough by themselves.
screen: `NO KING IN ISRAEL: A REFRAIN.` · `DEUTERONOMY: NOT IN YOUR OWN EYES.` · `SAMSON: SHE IS RIGHT IN MY EYES.` · `A KING, OR GOD AS KING?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: check one habit against more than your own eyes. Settle, and pick one habit you'd defend if anyone asked. How you spend the evening. How you talk when you're tired. How you spend money. Look at it through your own eyes first. Then through the eyes of someone it affects. Then, if you have one, through the eyes of your tradition. Just look. You don't have to change anything yet. The bell holds the time.
no king. The refrain of Judges' last chapters, about a time when everyone answered only to their own eyes. Today's word.
Your line: not just my own eyes. Today, before one decision, ask one other person how it looks to them. Tomorrow, the book of Samuel opens with a woman praying. Day seven hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: Jews read the closing verse of Judges as the hinge into the books of Samuel, and commentators differ on whether it calls for a human king or laments a people who no longer answered to God.

fork.setup: the book of Judges is closing. after a run of dark stories, what's the last line?
options: a song of thanks for the judges.
there was no king in Israel; every man did what was right in his own eyes.
a list of the tribes at peace.
fork.reveal: the book ends on the refrain, unresolved, and leaves the question open for the books of Samuel.

original.note: Hebrew: what is right in his eyes, the closing words of the book of Judges.

trapdoor: what you thought: a line praising people for following their conscience.
what it means: the book's closing warning about a time when everyone answered only to themselves.
what a scholar hears: Deuteronomy 12:8 uses the same phrase for what the people must stop doing, and Samson says it of the woman he wants (Judges 14:3).
recall: son of Abinoam, called to lead

sources.quoted: In those days there was no king in Israel; every man did that which was right in his own eyes.

notes: Audit: 'a warning about a single point of view' (a modern reduction that fits neither reading well) became 'people who answer to no one but themselves'; the fork no longer casts the listener as the book's editor (tradition, Bava Batra 14b, ascribes Judges to Samuel).
Verify JPS 1917 wording of Judges 21:25 (identical to the KJV as remembered).
The crime at Gibeah (Judges 19) is named only as 'a crime in a city at night' on purpose.
Judges 14:3 Hebrew 'hi yashrah ve'einai' (she is right in my eyes), rendered in the KJV 'she pleaseth me well'; please confirm.
The two readings of the refrain (a call for a king vs. God as king, via Gideon in 8:23) are offered without naming commentators.
Book boundary: Judges ends here; the carry points to Samuel and tomorrow's Hannah.

Editor: hook no longer opens on the generalization 'books usually end on a high note'; 'a tribe that steals another town's idol' corrected (Dan takes Micah's idols and his priest, Judges 18); the teach no longer says the full refrain comes only at the end (it also stands at 17:6); the closing lines are framed as the book's view, not the narrator's; review now names yesterday's line.
